mcqs.question: What happens if user-mode code attempts to write to a page marked read-only in its page-table entry?
options: The write silently succeeds but is discarded before reaching memory
The write succeeds, but the page's dirty bit is set to warn the OS
The OS is notified after the fact, once the write has already happened
Hardware detects the permission mismatch and triggers a fault before the write is allowed to complete
mcqs.explanation: Protection bits are checked by hardware before an access is permitted to proceed — a write to a read-only page is caught and faulted immediately, not silently discarded, not retroactively reported, and not allowed through with just a warning flag.

mcqs.question: How does a running program transition from user mode to kernel mode?
options: Only through tightly controlled mechanisms like a syscall instruction, interrupt, or exception, which hand control to a fixed OS-defined entry point
By setting a flag in its own memory that hardware trusts
By writing directly to the privilege-level register from user mode
It cannot happen at all once a program starts running
mcqs.explanation: Privilege escalation is only possible through specific, hardware-controlled mechanisms (syscall instructions, interrupts, exceptions) that transfer control to a fixed entry point the OS defines — arbitrary user code cannot simply flip its own privilege level or jump into kernel mode at will.

mcqs.question: Why can't memory protection rely on software convention alone (i.e. 'well-behaved programs just don't touch kernel memory')?
options: Because software conventions are always followed correctly in modern operating systems
Because a buggy or malicious program could otherwise directly access kernel memory, and protection must hold even against code actively trying to violate it
Because software conventions are faster to enforce than hardware checks
Because compilers already prevent any invalid memory access at compile time
mcqs.explanation: A real security boundary must hold even when code is buggy or actively malicious, not just when it's well-behaved — that's exactly why hardware enforces privilege levels and permission bits on every access rather than trusting software to police itself. Compilers cannot catch this at compile time for arbitrary or adversarial code, and enforcement isn't about speed.
